tips.title: Only electrons move
tips.body: Protons are held in the nuclei and never transfer by rubbing. So an object becomes **positive by losing electrons**, not by gaining protons. Any answer with protons moving is wrong however good the rest is.

tips.title: Equal and opposite, every time
tips.body: What one material gains, the other loses. If the rod is negative, the cloth is left **equally positive** — so a question asking about the cloth is answered by the rod, and it is one extra sentence for a mark.

tips.title: Four things in a field diagram
tips.body: Lines **all the way round**, an **arrow on each**, pointing **out of positive** and **into negative**, and **closer together near the sphere**. Check all four before moving on; each one is marked.

tips.title: Say without touching
tips.body: Evidence for a **non-contact** force needs the words *without touching* in it. Describing a rod swinging away is only half the mark — what makes it evidence is that the two rods never met.

tips.title: One explanation covers everything
tips.body: Charge creates a field → the field is stronger closer in → something in the field feels a force. Use it for attraction, repulsion, sparking and picking up paper; only the *something* changes.

why.matters:
Charge is usually invisible because everything around you holds equal amounts of both kinds, and they cancel. Rubbing two insulators upsets that by a tiny amount, moving electrons from one to the other, and the topic is about what that tiny imbalance does: a **force with nothing touching**, and a **field** reaching out from the charge that explains it.

The same picture scaled up is the crack from a car door and a lightning strike. Scaled down, it is how a photocopier draws a page.

examples.title: Why your hair stands up when you pull off a jumper
examples.body:
Dragging a jumper over your head rubs it against every hair, and electrons move between the two. Whichever way they go, every hair is left carrying the **same** kind of charge as its neighbours, and like charges repel.

A hair is light and free to move, so the push shows. Each one leans away from all the others, which is only possible by standing on end and fanning out. The crackle you hear is the same charge finding its way back as tiny sparks. On a damp day the charge leaks away through the moist air as fast as it forms, and nothing happens.

props.note: Every hair carries the same charge, so each pushes its neighbours away

visual.alt: Two like charges labelled as neighbouring hairs, with field lines showing them pushing apart, which is why charged hair stands on end

examples.title: The balloon that sticks to the wall
examples.body:
Rub a balloon on your hair and it gains electrons, so it is negatively charged. The wall is not charged at all, yet the balloon sticks to it.

The balloon's field reaches into the wall and pushes the wall's electrons a little further away, leaving the surface nearest the balloon slightly positive. Opposite charges attract, and that thin positive layer is enough to hold a balloon up. It is the charged rod picking up scraps of paper, with a wall for the paper. The balloon drops when its charge has leaked away, which takes minutes on a dry day and seconds on a humid one.

props.note: The wall has no charge overall; the balloon's field has shifted its electrons back

visual.alt: A negatively charged balloon beside the wall's surface, drawn with a positive charge because the balloon's field has pushed the wall's electrons away, with field lines showing the attraction

examples.title: How a photocopier draws with charge
examples.body:
A photocopier puts a page together out of static. A metal drum is given a charge all over. Light from the page, or a laser drawing it, lands on the drum where the page is **white**, and wherever light lands the drum conducts and the charge leaks away. The charge stays only where the page is **dark**.

Toner is a fine powder charged the opposite way, so it sticks only to the charged parts: the letters. Paper is pressed on, the toner moves across, and a hot roller melts it in. Charging, attraction of opposites, and charge leaking through a conductor: the whole topic, on a page.

steps.title: Rubbing moves electrons, not protons
steps.body:
When certain **insulating** materials are rubbed against each other, they become **electrically charged**.

The mechanism is worth stating exactly, because it is where the marks are:

**Negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.**

- The material that **gains** electrons becomes **negatively** charged.
- The material that **loses** electrons is left with an **equal positive** charge.

Two details matter and are easy to get wrong.

**Only electrons move.** Protons are held in the nuclei of atoms and do not move between the materials. So an object never becomes positive by gaining protons — it becomes positive by **losing electrons**. If your answer has protons moving, it is wrong however sensible the rest sounds.

**The charges are equal and opposite.** What one material gains, the other loses. Rub a polythene rod with a cloth and the rod gains, say, a certain number of electrons, becoming negative — and the cloth is left exactly as positive.

It happens with **insulators** because the charge cannot flow away. On a metal held in your hand, any charge would flow straight to earth.

steps.title: Attraction and repulsion
steps.body:
When two electrically charged objects are brought close together they **exert a force on each other**, and the rule is simple:

- Two objects carrying the **same** type of charge **repel**.
- Two objects carrying **different** types of charge **attract**.

These are **non-contact forces**: the objects push or pull each other **without touching**. Gravity and magnetism are the other two you have met.

**Evidence you can describe.** The spec asks for evidence that charged objects exert forces when not in contact, so have an example ready:

- Suspend a charged polythene rod so it can swing freely. Bring a second charged polythene rod near it **without touching** — the suspended rod swings **away**. Two like charges, so they repel.
- Bring a charged acetate rod near instead, and the suspended rod swings **towards** it. Different charges, so they attract.

The phrase *without touching* is what makes it evidence for a **non-contact** force, so say it.

A charged object will also attract **uncharged** objects — a charged rod picks up small pieces of paper. That is a separate effect, and it happens because the charge on the rod pulls the electrons in the paper slightly to one side.

steps.title: Electric fields
steps.body:
A charged object **creates an electric field around itself**. The field is the region where another charge would feel a force.

The two facts about its strength are:

- The electric field is **strongest close to the charged object**.
- **The further away, the weaker the field.**

And what the field does:

- A **second charged object placed in the field experiences a force**.
- **The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.**

This is how the idea of a field **explains** a non-contact force, which is what the spec asks you to do. Instead of saying two objects mysteriously push each other across a gap, you say: the first charge creates a field everywhere around it; the second charge sits **in** that field, and feels a force because of where it is. The force is then something happening **at** the second charge, not across empty space.

**Drawing the field for an isolated charged sphere** is a marked skill:

- Draw straight lines **radiating** from the sphere, evenly spaced all the way round.
- Put an **arrow on each line**. The arrows point **away from a positive** charge and **towards a negative** one.
- The lines are **closer together near the sphere**, which is how the drawing shows the field is stronger there.

steps.title: Sparking
steps.body:
**Sparking** is the phenomenon the spec asks you to describe and then to explain using fields, so it is worth doing properly.

**What happens.** As charge builds up on an object by rubbing, the **potential difference** between it and a nearby earthed object grows. When it is large enough, electrons jump across the gap through the air — a **spark**. You see it, hear it, and the object is left with much less charge.

**Explaining it with a field.** As the charge builds up, the electric field around the object gets **stronger**. Close to the object, and across a small gap, the field can become strong enough to pull electrons off the atoms in the **air**, so the air stops being an insulator and lets charge flow through it. That flow is the spark.

Two consequences follow, and both are examinable:

- The **smaller the gap**, the **stronger the field** for the same charge, so a spark happens at a **smaller** build-up of charge. That is why you feel a shock as your hand nears the door handle rather than while it is still far away.
- **Earthing** prevents sparks. A conducting path to earth lets the charge flow away steadily instead of building up, so the field never gets strong enough. This is why fuel tankers are earthed before fuel is transferred: a spark near fuel vapour would be dangerous.

steps.title: Going deeper: why a charged rod picks up paper
steps.body:
**The puzzle.** A charged rod attracts small pieces of paper, and the paper is **uncharged**. But the rule says attraction happens between **opposite** charges. So why does it work?

**The answer.** The rod's electric field acts on the charges **inside** the paper. Even though the paper has no overall charge, it contains equal numbers of positive and negative charges, and the field pulls them slightly in opposite directions. The side of the paper nearer the rod ends up with a small charge **opposite** to the rod's, and the far side with the same charge as the rod.

Now the nearer side is **closer** to the rod than the far side. The force is **stronger at smaller distances**, so the attraction of the near side beats the repulsion of the far side, and the paper is pulled in.

Notice what that argument needs: not just *opposite charges attract*, but **the force gets weaker with distance**. Both facts from this topic, used together. That combination is what a grade 9 answer looks like here.

**Being exact about charge.** Three phrasings lose marks:

- *The rod gains protons* — protons never move between materials. Only **electrons** move.
- *The rod gains charge* — vague. Say **electrons are transferred**, and say in which direction.
- *Static electricity builds up* — describes but does not explain. What builds up is **charge**, because electrons have been transferred and cannot flow away through an insulator.

**Why insulators.** Static builds up on insulators because the charge **cannot flow**. On a conductor, charge spreads out and flows to earth through whatever is holding it, so it does not accumulate. That is also why earthing works — it turns the object into part of a conducting path.

**One field, several phenomena.** The spec asks you to use the field idea to explain the non-contact force **and** other electrostatic phenomena such as sparking. It is the same explanation each time: charge creates a field; the field is stronger closer in; something in the field feels a force. For sparking, the something is the electrons in the air.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Rubbing certain **insulating** materials transfers **electrons** from one to the other.
- The material that **gains** electrons becomes **negative**; the one that **loses** them is left **equally positive**.
- **Only electrons move.** Protons stay in the nuclei, so nothing becomes positive by gaining protons.
- **Same charges repel; different charges attract**, and both are **non-contact** forces.
- Evidence: a suspended charged rod swings away from a like-charged rod brought near **without touching**.
- A charged object **creates an electric field** around itself.
- The field is **strongest close to the object** and **weaker further away**.
- A second charge **placed in the field experiences a force**, which **increases as they get closer**.
- To draw the field round a sphere: straight lines **all the way round**, an **arrow on each**, **away** from positive and **towards** negative, **closer together** near the sphere.
- **Sparking**: charge builds up, the field gets strong enough to break down the air, and charge jumps the gap.
- **Earthing** prevents it by letting charge flow away as it builds.
- A charged rod attracts **uncharged** paper because the field separates the charges inside it, and the nearer, opposite side is pulled more strongly than the far side is pushed.

questions.prompt: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain how the rod becomes charged, state what happens to the cloth, and describe an experiment that gives evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another without touching.
questions.solution: When the rod and the cloth are rubbed together, negatively charged electrons are rubbed off the cloth and on to the rod. Because the rod gains electrons it becomes negatively charged. The cloth has lost the same number of electrons, so it is left with an equal positive charge. It is important to note that only electrons move between the two materials, because protons are held within the nuclei of atoms and cannot be transferred by rubbing. The charge stays on the rod because polythene is an insulator, so the charge cannot flow away. To show that charged objects exert forces without touching, a charged polythene rod can be suspended so that it is free to swing. A second polythene rod, charged in the same way, is then brought close to it but without touching it. The suspended rod swings away from the second rod, showing that two objects with the same type of charge repel one another. If instead a positively charged acetate rod is brought near, the suspended rod swings towards it, showing that different charges attract. Because the rods never touch, this is evidence of a non-contact force.

questions.modelAnswer:
**How the rod becomes charged.** Rubbing transfers **negatively charged electrons** from the cloth **on to the rod**. Gaining electrons makes the rod **negative**.

**What happens to the cloth.** It has **lost** the same number of electrons, so it is left with an **equal positive** charge. Charge is conserved: what one gains, the other loses.

**Only electrons move.** Protons are held in the **nuclei** and cannot be transferred by rubbing. An object becomes positive by **losing electrons**, never by gaining protons.

The charge stays put because polythene is an **insulator**, so it cannot flow away.

**The experiment.**

1. **Suspend** a charged polythene rod so it can swing freely.
2. Bring a second polythene rod, charged the same way, **close to it but without touching**.
3. The suspended rod swings **away**: two like charges **repel**.
4. Repeat with a positively charged acetate rod: the suspended rod swings **towards** it — different charges **attract**.

The rods **never touch**, so this is evidence of a **non-contact** force. Say *without touching* explicitly: it is what makes the observation evidence rather than a description.

questions.prompt: Explain what an electric field is, describe how to draw the field around an isolated negatively charged sphere, and use the idea of a field to explain why a spark can jump from a charged object to an earthed one.
questions.solution: A charged object creates an electric field in the space around itself. The field is a region in which another charged object would experience a force. The field is strongest close to the charged object and becomes weaker the further away from it you go. To draw the field around an isolated negatively charged sphere, draw straight lines radiating outwards from the sphere in all directions, evenly spaced all the way round it, and put an arrow on each line. For a negative charge the arrows point inwards, towards the sphere. The lines should be drawn closer together near the sphere, because that is where the field is strongest. A spark can be explained using the same idea. As charge builds up on an object, the electric field around it becomes stronger. If the field becomes strong enough it pulls electrons off the atoms in the air in the gap, so the air stops behaving as an insulator and instead conducts. Charge then flows through the air across the gap, which is the spark. The smaller the gap, the stronger the field for a given charge, so a spark jumps more readily across a small gap.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What an electric field is.** A charged object **creates an electric field** in the space around itself: the region in which **another charge would experience a force**. It is **strongest close to** the object and **weaker further away**.

**Drawing it for a negative sphere.**

- Straight lines **radiating outwards**, evenly spaced **all the way round**.
- An **arrow on each line**, pointing **inwards** — towards a negative charge.
- Lines **closer together near the sphere**, showing the field is strongest there.

**Explaining a spark.**

1. As charge builds up on the object, the field around it becomes **stronger**.
2. When it is strong enough, it **pulls electrons off the atoms in the air** in the gap.
3. The air stops being an insulator and **conducts**.
4. Charge flows across the gap — the **spark**.

The **smaller the gap**, the stronger the field for a given charge, so a spark jumps more readily across a small gap. That is why the shock comes as your hand is almost at the door handle.

Note the same three-step shape as every field explanation in this topic: charge creates a field, the field is stronger closer in, and something in the field feels a force. Here the something is the electrons in the air.

examTechnique.body:
Name the particle that moves and the direction it moved in. Electrons, and from which material to which.

Say what happens to both objects, not just the one the question names. The charges are equal and opposite.

For a field diagram, draw lines all the way round with arrows on them, and make them closer together near the sphere. Out of positive, into negative.

When a question says explain rather than state, use the field: the charge creates a field, the field is stronger closer in, and a charge in the field feels a force.

For evidence of a non-contact force, describe what was observed and say that the objects did not touch.

For sparking, link a growing charge to a stronger field, and the stronger field to the air breaking down.

Saying an object gains a positive charge rather than losing electrons.
Forgetting that the other material is left with an equal and opposite charge.
Drawing field lines on only one side of the sphere.
Drawing field lines with no arrows on them.
Pointing the arrows outwards from a negative charge.
Describing a spark without saying the field breaks down the air.
Leaving out without touching when giving evidence for a non-contact force.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer names the particle and its direction in the first sentence, then says what the other object is left with without being asked. Its field diagrams have all four features because it checks them rather than recalling them. Asked to explain rather than state, it reaches for the field every time — charge makes a field, the field is stronger closer in, something in the field feels a force — and uses the same three steps for attraction, sparking and a rod picking up paper. For the paper it combines two facts rather than one, noticing that the near side is closer and the force falls with distance, which is what makes the attraction win.
